title: LegosTracker: LEGO sets as a market

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Would a LEGO set from 1965 have been a good investment? LegosTracker looks at LEGO sets the way you'd look at a market, to find out.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Ha, I like it. Where does the data come from?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Two places. The Rebrickable catalog says which sets, parts and themes exist, and a scraper adds the prices those sets fetch over time from BrickEconomy. It's an AlgoÉTS data project, all in Python and Jupyter notebooks.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It reads a list of set numbers and drives a visible Chromium window with Playwright. For each set, it searches BrickEconomy, opens the matching page and pulls out the chart data hidden in the page's script.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: The value history goes into one file per set, and when a four-band price series exists, that gets its own file. Then it reads the details, pricing, quick buy, predictions and facts panels into structured models and adds them all to one big table.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So that's the collecting. What about the analysis?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: One notebook explores the Rebrickable tables, colours, parts, sets and themes, and plots counts. Another cleans the scraped prices and focuses on set zero zero one dash one, the one from 1965. It fits a linear model and a gradient boosting model on its price history and projects both to 2030.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: There's also a Monte Carlo simulation on the log returns, and charts of yearly gains and of the four price bands. It's a nice little tour of different ways to think about the same price curve.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Does it work for someone's own bricks, too?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It does. A third notebook takes a personal collection file, looks up each set's retail price and current value on BrickEconomy, and writes an updated file.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So collectors and data-curious people both get something.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's the idea. The blog article tells the story with charts, and the project page lists every notebook.
